posts.title: FEMA and foreign investment in simple words
posts.excerpt: The basic rules when a foreign person invests in an Indian company.
posts.body:
The Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) governs foreign exchange and foreign investment in India. The details are in the Rules and Regulations framed by the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India.

## Entry routes

- Under the automatic route, no prior government approval is needed.
- Under the government route, approval is needed first.
- Some sectors have a cap on foreign holding or have conditions.

## Pricing and reporting

- Shares generally must be issued or transferred at a price that follows the pricing guidelines.
- The company must report the investment to the RBI through an authorised bank within the time limit, which for allotment is 30 days, using the FIRMS portal and the form prescribed.
- The company must also file annual returns of foreign liabilities and assets.

## Why it matters

- Breaking the rules can lead to penalties and compounding applications to the RBI.

Sector caps and procedures are revised often, so the latest FDI policy and regulations should be checked. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Copyright in simple words
posts.excerpt: What copyright protects and how long it lasts.
posts.body:
Copyright is a right given to the creator of an original work. In India it is governed by the Copyright Act, 1957.

## What it protects

- Literary works, including software, artistic works, music, films and sound recordings.
- It protects the expression, not an idea or a method.

## Registration

- Copyright arises automatically when the work is created. Registration is not compulsory, but a registration certificate is useful evidence in a dispute.
- Applications are made to the Copyright Office.

## How long

- For most works, copyright lasts for the life of the author and sixty years after death. The period differs for some works, such as films and sound recordings.

## Rights and exceptions

- The owner can copy, adapt, publish and license the work.
- The Act allows fair dealing for research, criticism and some other purposes.
- The author also has moral rights, and ownership can change through assignment in writing.

A written agreement is the best way to make clear who owns a work created for a business. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Patents in simple words
posts.excerpt: What can be patented and the basic process.
posts.body:
A patent gives the inventor an exclusive right over a new invention for a limited period, in return for disclosing it to the public. In India it is governed by the Patents Act, 1970.

## What can be patented

- The invention must be new, involve an inventive step and be capable of industrial application.
- Some things are not patentable under the Act, such as mere discoveries, mathematical methods and certain computer programs as such.

## Process in short

- File the application, with a provisional or complete specification, at the Patent Office.
- The application is published, generally after eighteen months from filing.
- A request for examination must be made, and objections raised in the examination report must be answered.
- If all is in order, the patent is granted.

## Duration

- A patent is valid for twenty years from the date of filing, subject to payment of the renewal fees every year.

## Remember

- Public disclosure before filing can destroy novelty.
- Protection is only in India. Foreign protection needs filings in other countries.

A patent search before filing helps check novelty. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Design registration in simple words
posts.excerpt: Protecting the look of a product.
posts.body:
A design registration protects the shape, pattern, ornament or colour scheme of a product that appeals to the eye. It does not protect how the product works. In India it is governed by the Designs Act, 2000.

## What qualifies

- The design must be new and original and must not have been published before filing.
- It must be applied to an article, such as a bottle, a chair or a fabric pattern.

## Process

- File the application with representations of the design at the Designs Office.
- The Controller examines and may raise objections.
- If accepted, the design is registered and published.

## Duration

- The registration lasts for ten years from the date of registration, and can be extended once for five more years, giving a total of fifteen years.

## Remember

- Showing the design in public before filing can affect its novelty.
- For functional features, a patent is the right route.

The same product can have a design, a trademark and copyright working together. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Trademark opposition and renewal in simple words
posts.excerpt: What happens when someone objects to your mark and how to keep it alive.
posts.body:
After a trademark is published in the Journal, the process does not stop. Others have a chance to oppose, and the owner must also renew the registration on time.

## Opposition

- Anyone can file a notice of opposition within four months of publication, which can be extended by one more month on request.
- The applicant must file a counter-statement within the time set, or the application can be treated as abandoned.
- Both sides file evidence, and a hearing is held before the Registrar.

## Renewal

- A registration is valid for ten years and can be renewed for further periods of ten years.
- The renewal request can be filed up to six months before expiry.
- If it is missed, there is a period in which it can be renewed with a surcharge. After that, the mark can be removed from the register and a restoration application is needed.

## Tips

- Keep a diary of deadlines.
- Use the mark regularly, since non-use for a long period can expose it to removal.

Procedures and fees change, so the Registry website should be checked for each step. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Geographical Indications (GI) in simple words
posts.excerpt: Protection for products linked to a place.
posts.body:
A Geographical Indication identifies goods that come from a particular place and whose quality, reputation or character is due to that place. Examples seen in India include Darjeeling tea and Banarasi sarees. The law is the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999.

## Who can apply

- An association of persons, a producers' organisation or an authority established by law, representing the interests of the producers.

## Process

- File an application with the GI Registry, with the map, the description and the standards of production.
- It is examined, published, and open to objection.
- If accepted, the GI is registered.

## Duration and use

- The registration lasts for ten years and can be renewed.
- Authorised users of the area register as such users and may use the GI on their goods.
- An individual cannot own a GI.

A GI protects a community's name and quality, not a single business. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: IP licence and assignment in simple words
posts.excerpt: Two ways to let another person use or own your intellectual property.
posts.body:
Owning intellectual property such as a trademark, patent or copyright does not mean you must use it alone. You can give others the right to use it, or transfer it. The two are different.

## Assignment

- Ownership is permanently transferred to another person.
- It should be in writing, and for the registered IPs, it has to be recorded in the proper registry.

## Licence

- The owner keeps the ownership and permits another to use the IP, on terms.
- The terms can cover the territory, the period, exclusivity, payment of royalty, quality control and termination.

## Things to include

- A clear description of the IP and the rights given.
- Rules on improvements, confidentiality and what happens when the agreement ends.
- Which law and court will apply.

## Tax and stamp duty

- Royalty and transfer payments can have tax, GST and stamp duty effects, so these should be checked before signing.

A well drafted agreement avoids later disputes over who owns what. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Legal notice in simple words
posts.excerpt: What a legal notice is and what a good one contains.
posts.body:
A legal notice is a formal written communication, sent before taking a matter to court or another forum. It tells the other side what the complaint is and what is demanded. For some matters, such as suits against the government under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure, a notice is required by law.

## A good notice contains

- The names and addresses of the parties.
- The facts in order, with dates.
- The legal ground and the demand, for example payment or stopping an act.
- A reasonable time to comply, and the action that will follow if there is no response.

## Sending

- It is sent by a method that gives proof of delivery, such as registered post or email with proof, and a copy is kept.

## If you receive one

- Read it carefully, do not ignore it, and note the date.
- Collect your documents and reply in writing within the time given.

A notice is not a court order, but the reply and the records can matter later. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: What a good business agreement contains, in simple words
posts.excerpt: The key parts of a contract that prevent disputes.
posts.body:
A written agreement records what the parties have agreed. Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a valid contract needs offer, acceptance, lawful consideration and lawful object, between parties who are able to contract. A clear document makes the terms easy to prove.

## Basic parts

- Parties and date.
- Scope of work or goods, with price and payment terms.
- Time and place of delivery or performance.
- Warranties and the standard of quality.

## Protective clauses

- Confidentiality and intellectual property ownership.
- Termination and what happens after.
- Liability limits and indemnity.
- Dispute resolution, such as arbitration or court jurisdiction, and the governing law.

## Practical tips

- Use simple, specific words. Avoid unclear terms.
- Check stamp duty rules of the state, because an unstamped document may not be admitted as evidence until duty and penalty are paid.
- Sign every page, and keep original copies.

A template should always be adjusted to the actual deal. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Year-end checklist for importers, exporters and companies
posts.excerpt: A simple list of things to review as the year closes.
posts.body:
The end of the year is a good time to check that records are in order. This list is general and each business should adapt it.

## Trade side

- Check that the IEC is active and the details are current.
- List open authorisations, such as Advance Authorisation or EPCG, with their export obligation dates.
- Check pending refunds, bonds and bank guarantees.
- Review whether any anti-dumping or other duty changed for your goods.
- Check validity of BIS, EPR, or other certificates.

## Company side

- Note the due dates of the annual forms and the board and general meetings.
- Review the registers, and update the directors' details.
- Check shareholder records and any foreign investment reporting.

## IP and contracts

- List trademarks, designs and patents with renewal dates.
- Check agreements that expire or renew soon.

## Records

- Keep customs and GST papers safely for the periods the law requires, in a place that can be found easily.

A short review now can avoid a late fee or a missed deadline in the new year. Rules, fees and procedures change, so the current law, notification or official portal should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: India's trade agreements at a glance: complete list and status (FTA notes 1)
posts.excerpt: All the free trade and preferential trade agreements of India, in force, signed, concluded and under negotiation.
posts.body:
India has trade agreements of several kinds. A Free Trade Agreement (FTA) or Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) cuts duty on most goods between the partners. A Preferential Trade Agreement (PTA) cuts duty on a smaller list of goods. Status below is as published in trackers updated in October and November 2026.

## In force: free trade and economic partnership agreements

- Sri Lanka FTA, in force 1 March 2000.
- SAFTA (South Asia), in force 1 January 2006.
- Thailand Early Harvest Scheme, in force 1 September 2004, covering only the early-harvest list.
- Singapore CECA, in force 1 August 2005.
- ASEAN goods agreement (AITIGA), in force 2010, and the services and investment agreements, in force 1 July 2015. The goods agreement is under review.
- South Korea CEPA, in force 1 January 2010, with an upgrade under negotiation.
- Japan CEPA, in force 1 August 2011.
- Malaysia CECA, in force 1 July 2011.
- Mauritius CECPA, in force 1 April 2021.
- UAE CEPA, in force 1 May 2022.
- Australia ECTA (interim), in force 29 December 2022.
- EFTA TEPA (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland), signed 10 March 2024, in force 1 October 2025.
- United Kingdom CETA, in force 15 July 2026.
- Oman CEPA, in force 1 June 2026.
- New Zealand FTA, in force 20 October 2026.

## In force: treaties and preferential agreements

- Nepal Treaty of Trade and Bhutan Agreement on Trade, Commerce and Transit.
- APTA (Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement).
- GSTP (Global System of Trade Preferences among developing countries).
- SAPTA, Afghanistan PTA, MERCOSUR PTA and Chile PTA.

## Concluded but not yet in force

- European Union FTA, concluded 27 January 2026. Signing and approvals were still pending in the trackers I checked.

## Under negotiation or discussion

- United States (a framework for an interim agreement was announced in February 2026), Canada, Chile (widening the PTA), Israel, the Gulf Cooperation Council, Maldives, Peru, Philippines, the Eurasian Economic Union, Australia (a fuller CECA), South Korea (upgrade), Mexico, SACU, Egypt, Qatar and Sri Lanka (ETCA).

## Next notes in this series

- How to claim benefit under an FTA, then notes on each group of agreements.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: How to claim benefit under an FTA: origin, proof and risks (FTA notes 2)
posts.excerpt: The common steps for an importer or exporter: origin criteria, proof of origin, direct shipment and verification.
posts.body:
A trade agreement gives a lower duty only to goods that 'originate' in the partner country. The benefit is not automatic. It has to be claimed and proved.

## Step 1: check that the goods are covered

- Find the HS code and check the tariff schedule of the agreement for that code. A product can be covered in one agreement and not in another.
- Check the duty rate for the year of import, because many schedules cut duty in stages.

## Step 2: check the origin rule

- Each agreement has product-specific rules. Common tests are 'wholly obtained', a change in tariff heading, and a regional or local value content percentage.
- Some agreements allow cumulation, which means inputs from other partner countries can count as local.

## Step 3: get the proof of origin

- Under many older agreements, a certificate of origin is issued by an authority of the exporting country.
- Under some newer agreements, the exporter or producer gives an origin declaration instead. The UK CETA and the draft EU text were reported to move in this direction.
- Electronic certificates are now accepted in some agreements. For example, a protocol with MERCOSUR signed in September 2026 gives electronic certificates the same standing as paper ones.

## Step 4: meet the shipment condition

- Goods usually must be shipped directly from the partner. Transit through a third country is allowed only on the terms of the agreement.
- Under the India-UAE CEPA, as an example, passing through a Gulf port does not give origin.

## Step 5: file the claim

- The preferential rate is claimed in the Bill of Entry with the notification number and the origin documents.

## Verification and risk

- India's Customs (Administration of Rules of Origin under Trade Agreements) Rules, 2020, known as CAROTAR, require the importer to hold information that shows the origin conditions are met, and customs can ask for it.
- If origin is not proved, the benefit can be denied, with duty, interest and penalty.

## Records to keep

- Supplier's cost sheet and bill of materials, invoices, certificates and shipping papers, for the period the law requires.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

posts.title: India's agreements in Asia: ASEAN, Japan, Korea, Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand (FTA notes 3)
posts.excerpt: Detailed notes on India's older FTAs and CEPAs with East and South-East Asian partners.
posts.body:
These are India's oldest comprehensive trade agreements. Several are being reviewed or upgraded.

## ASEAN (AITIGA)

- Partners: the ten ASEAN member states.
- Goods agreement signed 13 August 2009 and in force in 2010, with the date differing country by country. Services and investment agreements were signed in November 2014 and are in force from 1 July 2015.
- The goods agreement is under review. In September 2026, ministers reviewed progress and aimed for a substantial conclusion in 2026. Reports also mention concern about misuse of rules of origin.

## Japan CEPA

- Signed 16 February 2011, in force 1 August 2011.
- Product-specific tariff concessions and origin rules apply.
- Talks on modernisation continue, mainly on services and the trade imbalance. A Joint Committee met in Tokyo on 2 March 2026.

## South Korea CEPA

- Signed 7 August 2009, in force 1 January 2010.
- An upgrade is under negotiation. The twelfth round was held in May 2026, covering goods, services, rules of origin, origin procedures, investment and sanitary and phytosanitary measures. Automotive and safeguard clauses are under review.

## Singapore CECA

- Signed 29 June 2005, in force 1 August 2005.
- It covers goods, services and investment together.

## Malaysia CECA

- Signed 18 February 2011, in force 1 July 2011.

## Thailand Early Harvest Scheme

- Signed 9 October 2003, in force 1 September 2004.
- Only the early-harvest product list gets a concession. A full FTA with Thailand has not been concluded.

## Practical tip

- The same product can have different duty rates and origin rules under ASEAN, Japan and Korea. Compare before choosing the source country, and check which one gives the proof the supplier can actually provide.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

posts.title: India's agreements in South Asia and the developing world: SAFTA, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Bhutan, APTA, GSTP (FTA notes 4)
posts.excerpt: Notes on the regional and developing-country trade agreements.
posts.body:
India has several regional trade arrangements with neighbours and with other developing countries.

## India-Sri Lanka FTA

- Signed 28 December 1998, in force 1 March 2000.
- A wider economic and technology cooperation agreement (ETCA) is still under discussion.

## SAFTA

- South Asian Free Trade Area among SAARC members. Signed 4 January 2004, in force 1 January 2006, with tariff concessions from 1 July 2006.
- It evolved from the earlier SAPTA, which was signed on 11 April 1993 and in force from 7 December 1995.

## Nepal

- Treaty of Trade signed 27 October 2009. It renews for seven-year terms unless either side gives three months' notice.

## Bhutan

- Agreement on Trade, Commerce and Transit, renewed on 12 November 2016 and in force from 29 July 2017 for ten years, so its term runs to July 2027.

## Afghanistan PTA

- Signed 6 March 2003, in force 13 May 2003.

## APTA

- Asia-Pacific Trade Agreement. Members include Bangladesh, China, Korea, Lao PDR, Mongolia and Sri Lanka along with India. Revised on 2 November 2005.

## GSTP

- Global System of Trade Preferences among developing countries. Signed 13 April 1988, in force 19 April 1989.

## Practical tip

- Some of these agreements cover only a limited list of goods, and a few have special rules, so product-level checks are essential.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

posts.title: India's agreements with the UAE, Oman, Mauritius, Australia and New Zealand (FTA notes 5)
posts.excerpt: Detailed notes on India's newer agreements with Gulf, African and Pacific partners.
posts.body:
These agreements were negotiated in the last few years and are broader than the older ones. They include services and other areas.

## UAE CEPA

- Signed 18 February 2022, in force 1 May 2022.
- Tariff cuts on most tariff lines.
- Origin requires production or sufficient processing in the UAE. Passing through a Gulf port does not give origin.

## Oman CEPA

- Signed 18 December 2025, in force 1 June 2026.
- Oman gives duty-free access on about 98% of its tariff lines, covering about 99.4% of India's exports by value, as reported. India offers concessions on about 78% of its tariff lines.
- Sensitive products are subject to tariff-rate quotas and minimum import prices. The agreement also covers services and professional mobility.

## Mauritius CECPA

- Signed 22 February 2021, in force 1 April 2021. It is described as India's first trade agreement with an African country.

## Australia ECTA

- Interim Economic Cooperation and Trade Agreement, signed 2 April 2022 and in force 29 December 2022.
- Talks on a fuller CECA continue.

## New Zealand FTA

- Signed in April 2026 (trackers give 24 or 27 April), in force 20 October 2026.
- New Zealand is reported to remove tariffs on all its tariff lines for Indian goods. India offers concessions on about 70% of its tariff lines, covering about 95% of trade value, as reported.
- Rules of origin were notified by CBIC on 12 October 2026, with product-specific criteria.

posts.title: India's agreements with the UK, EFTA and the European Union (FTA notes 6)
posts.excerpt: Detailed notes on the UK CETA, the EFTA TEPA and the EU FTA.
posts.body:
These are among India's largest and newest agreements, with high-income partners.

## United Kingdom CETA

- Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, signed 24 July 2025, in force 15 July 2026 together with a social security agreement.
- Indian exports get preferential access on about 99% of UK tariff lines, as reported. India cuts or removes duty on about 90% of its tariff lines.
- Sectors named include textiles, leather, gems and jewellery, engineering, marine, chemicals and processed foods.
- Proof of origin is an exporter or producer declaration instead of a certificate.
- A quota for UK vehicle imports applies for each calendar year, and applications for 2027 were reported to be open in November 2026.

## EFTA TEPA

- Trade and Economic Partnership Agreement with Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland. Signed 10 March 2024 and in force 1 October 2025.
- EFTA gives better access on about 92% of its tariff lines, covering most Indian exports, as reported. It also includes an investment commitment by EFTA.

## European Union FTA

- Negotiations were concluded on 27 January 2026.
- In the trackers checked, signing and the approvals of the European Council and Parliament were still pending, with a signing around December 2026 reported as expected.
- It is expected to cut tariffs in phases on goods and to cover services. It is not in force, so it should not be claimed yet.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

posts.title: Chile, MERCOSUR and agreements under negotiation (FTA notes 7)
posts.excerpt: The PTAs in the Americas and the list of agreements still being negotiated.
posts.body:
Besides agreements in force, India is negotiating many more. These cannot be used yet, but they show where trade rules may change.

## In force

- India-Chile PTA, signed 8 March 2006 and in force 11 September 2007, expanded in 2017. A wider CEPA is being negotiated.
- India-MERCOSUR PTA (Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay), signed 25 January 2004 and in force 1 June 2009, with limited concessions. A protocol signed in September 2026 gives electronic certificates of origin equal standing, without changing concessions.

## Under negotiation

- United States: a framework for an interim agreement was announced in February 2026. Talks continue.
- Canada: CEPA negotiations launched 2 March 2026, with a stated aim to conclude by the end of 2026.
- Mexico: terms of reference signed on 28 October 2026.
- Gulf Cooperation Council: FTA process launched in February 2026.
- Israel, Maldives, Peru, Philippines, Eurasian Economic Union, the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), Egypt and Qatar are at various stages.
- Australia (fuller CECA), South Korea (upgrade) and Chile (CEPA) are upgrades of existing agreements.

## What it means for a business

- Do not claim any benefit under an agreement that is not in force.
- Watch for CBIC notifications, because origin rules are notified separately before a benefit can be claimed.

Status and terms are taken from published trackers and may have changed. The agreement text, the Department of Commerce website and the CBIC notifications should be checked before any claim.

posts.title: Re-import of exported goods in simple words
posts.excerpt: What happens when goods sent abroad come back to India.
posts.body:
Sometimes goods that were exported return to India, for example because a buyer rejected them or they were sent for repair. Customs treats this as an import, but the law has special provisions to avoid charging full duty twice.

## Common situations

- Goods returned because of rejection, damage or a cancelled order.
- Goods sent abroad for repair, testing or exhibition and brought back.
- Goods exported under a scheme, where the export benefit may need to be paid back.

## What is usually required

- Proof that the goods were exported from India, such as the shipping bill and export invoice.
- A bill of entry for the re-import with the reason for return.
- Any benefit taken on the export, such as drawback or a refund, may have to be returned with the duty rules applying.

## Points to watch

- Time limits for re-import apply under the relevant notification.
- Records should link the original export to the return.

The notification that grants the concession should be read for the exact conditions. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Customs broker in simple words
posts.excerpt: Who a customs broker is and what the importer remains responsible for.
posts.body:
A customs broker is a person licensed by customs to deal with customs authorities on behalf of an importer or exporter. The licence is given under section 146 of the Customs Act, 1962 and the Customs Brokers Licensing Regulations, 2018.

## What a broker does

- Files bills of entry and shipping bills.
- Pays duty, arranges examination and takes delivery of cargo.
- Advises on documents and procedure.

## What the broker must do under the Regulations

- Know the client and verify the identity of the importer or exporter.
- Exercise due diligence about the correctness of the information given.
- Keep records and not let others use the licence.

## What the importer should know

- The importer is still responsible for the declaration and for the duty.
- A written authorisation to the broker should be given.
- Keep copies of everything filed on your behalf.

A good working relationship with documents shared in advance prevents most errors. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Provisional assessment in simple words
posts.excerpt: Clearing goods before the final duty is decided.
posts.body:
Sometimes the importer cannot say what the final duty is at the time of import, for example because the price is yet to be settled or a test report is awaited. Section 18 of the Customs Act, 1962 allows goods to be released on provisional assessment.

## When it can be used

- When the importer cannot produce documents needed for assessment.
- When the goods need chemical or other tests.
- When the value or classification is under enquiry.

## How it works

- The importer gives a bond, often with security, for the difference between provisional and final duty.
- The officer later finalises the assessment, and either collects the extra duty with interest or refunds the excess.

## Points to remember

- Finalisation should happen within the time limit in the Act, and delays can be raised with the department.
- The bond remains in force until finalisation.

It helps cash flow but keeps the matter open, so the bond and timelines should be tracked. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Examination and testing of imported goods in simple words
posts.excerpt: What happens when customs examines or samples your cargo.
posts.body:
After a bill of entry is filed, the officer may decide to examine the goods or take samples. This is a normal part of customs control under the Customs Act, 1962.

## Examination

- It may be physical, or by scanner, depending on the risk assessment of the system.
- The importer or broker is present to open packages and identify the goods.

## Testing

- Samples may be sent to a customs or other recognised laboratory for classification or compliance checks.
- The test report can affect duty, and where the importer disagrees, a re-test may be requested.

## What the importer can do

- Keep complete product literature and specifications ready.
- Ask for a copy of the test report, and reply in writing to any query.

Delays in testing can cause storage charges, so documents should be ready before arrival. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Export proceeds and realisation in simple words
posts.excerpt: Why money from an export must come back to India.
posts.body:
Under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 and the regulations made under it, an exporter must bring the export proceeds back to India within the period prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India.

## The basics

- Exports should be made against a proper invoice and shipping bill.
- Proceeds are generally to be received through an authorised dealer bank and the bank records the realisation against the shipping bill.
- The time limit for realisation is set by the RBI and has been changed from time to time.

## If the money is delayed

- An extension can be asked for through the bank in cases where the law allows.
- Failure to realise within time can lead to action under FEMA.

## Why it matters for schemes

- Many export schemes need proof of realisation before the benefit or the discharge certificate is given.

The current RBI directions on the period of realisation should be checked. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Export of services in simple words
posts.excerpt: What counts as an export of services and why it matters for tax.
posts.body:
When an Indian business provides services to a client outside India, it can be an export of services. This matters mainly for GST, where such exports can be zero-rated, and for foreign exchange rules.

## The conditions in short

- The supplier is in India and the recipient is outside India.
- The place of supply is outside India.
- Payment is received in convertible foreign exchange or in Indian rupees where the RBI permits.
- The supplier and recipient are not merely establishments of the same person.

## Where the rules are

- Section 2(6) of the Integrated GST Act, 2017 defines export of services.
- RBI rules govern receipt of payment.

## Practical points

- Keep contracts, invoices and bank realisation certificates.
- Claim a refund or use a letter of undertaking as the GST rules provide.

The definition has several conditions, and each must be met. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: FTP, Handbook and notifications: how to read them together
posts.excerpt: Which document rules which question.
posts.body:
Foreign trade law has several layers, and it helps to know which one answers your question.

## Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992

- The parent Act that gives the Central Government the power to regulate trade and issue the policy.

## Foreign Trade Policy

- States the policy and schemes in broad terms.

## Handbook of Procedures

- Gives the procedure and forms to apply under the policy.

## Notifications and public notices

- Change the policy or procedure during the year. They carry the latest text.
- ITC(HS) classification shows whether goods are free, restricted or prohibited.

## Customs notifications

- CBIC notifications give duty rates and exemptions. A DGFT scheme usually needs both a DGFT authorisation and a CBIC exemption.

## Habit to build

- Read the policy provision, then the procedure, then check for later notices.

Amendments are published often, so the latest versions should be used. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Status Holder recognition in simple words
posts.excerpt: Recognition for exporters with a good export record.
posts.body:
The Foreign Trade Policy recognises exporters with a sufficient export performance as Status Holders, such as One Star Export House and higher grades. The recognition brings some facilitation.

## How it works

- Status depends on export performance over a period, measured in US dollars.
- The exporter applies on the DGFT portal with proof of exports.

## Typical benefits

- Simpler procedures for some authorisations, and self-certification in certain cases.
- The exact benefits are listed in the Foreign Trade Policy and Handbook.

## Remember

- The thresholds and benefits change with each policy, so they should be read from the current text.

Recognition is for a block of years and needs a fresh application when it ends. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Deemed exports in simple words
posts.excerpt: Supplies within India that are treated like exports.
posts.body:
Some supplies of goods within India are treated as exports under the Foreign Trade Policy, even though the goods do not leave the country. These are called deemed exports.

## Examples in general

- Supply of goods to an export oriented unit or a unit in a special economic zone, where the policy says so.
- Supply against an advance authorisation or against EPCG in the cases listed.

## Why it matters

- The supplier or the recipient can claim certain benefits, such as refund of duty or exemption from it, as the policy provides.
- GST treatment has its own rules.

## Procedure

- Claims are made through the DGFT portal with the supply documents and certificates.
- Time limits for claims apply.

The list of deemed exports and the benefits are in the current policy and should be checked. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Provisional release of seized goods in simple words
posts.excerpt: Getting goods back on a bond while the case continues.
posts.body:
If customs seizes goods, they can sometimes be released before the case is decided. This is called provisional release and is provided in section 110A of the Customs Act, 1962.

## How it works

- The owner applies to the proper officer.
- The officer may release the goods on a bond and security, and on conditions about the amount.
- The goods remain subject to the final order.

## Why use it

- Goods such as perishable items or machinery lose value or block business while waiting.

## Points to remember

- Not every kind of goods can be released. Prohibited goods are treated differently.
- If the case is later lost, the bond and security can be enforced.

A seizure should be responded to quickly, with the documents ready. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Bonds and bank guarantees under customs in simple words
posts.excerpt: The promises you give customs when a scheme needs them.
posts.body:
Several customs schemes, such as bonded warehousing, MOOWR and export schemes, require the importer to sign a bond and sometimes give a bank guarantee. This is the importer's promise to follow the conditions.

## What a bond is

- A legal undertaking to pay a stated amount if the conditions are not met.
- Its amount is tied to the duty at stake, with a margin as the rules fix.

## What a guarantee is

- Security from a bank that customs can claim if the importer fails.

## Practical points

- Keep track of when each bond expires, and apply for its release after the conditions are done.
- Pay attention to the format and the bank's validity period.
- Keep proof of release.

A bond that is not discharged can stay as a liability on the books. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Uncleared imported goods in simple words
posts.excerpt: What happens when imported goods are not cleared in time.
posts.body:
If imported goods are not cleared within the time allowed, the Customs Act, 1962 allows customs to deal with them. Section 48 deals with goods not cleared within the permitted period after being unloaded.

## What can happen

- After the period, the goods can be sold after notice, and the proceeds are used first to pay duty, charges and expenses.
- Some goods have shorter periods, for example perishable goods.

## What the importer can do

- Clear the goods quickly, or apply for extension where the rules permit.
- Seek permission to warehouse or re-export where the law allows.

## Costs

- Storage and demurrage charges can be heavy, so delays should be avoided.

Time limits are short, so a clearance plan should be ready before the shipment arrives. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Section 8 company in simple words
posts.excerpt: A company formed for charitable or similar objects.
posts.body:
A Section 8 company is a company formed for promoting commerce, art, science, education, sports, charity or similar objects, which applies its profits to those objects and does not pay dividends to members. It is provided in section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013.

## Key features

- It needs a licence from the Central Government, which is applied for through the MCA portal.
- Profits and income must be used only for the objects. No dividend is paid to members.
- The name usually ends with 'Foundation' or similar, and the word 'Limited' or 'Private Limited' may be dropped as the rules permit.

## Compliance

- Annual accounts and returns are filed like any company.
- The licence can be revoked if the conditions are broken.

## Tax and other laws

- Tax exemption needs separate registration under the Income-tax Act.

It suits non-profit work, not a business that wants to distribute profit. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Board meetings and minutes in simple words
posts.excerpt: The basic rules for how directors meet and record decisions.
posts.body:
Directors make decisions as a board, and the Companies Act, 2013 and the Secretarial Standards set out how meetings should be held and recorded.

## Meetings

- A board meeting must be held at least four times a year, with a gap between meetings as the Act requires.
- Notice must be given to every director, with the agenda.
- A quorum must be present for the meeting to be valid.

## Minutes

- Minutes record what was decided, who attended and any dissent.
- They are signed by the chairperson and kept in a minutes book.
- Papers placed before the meeting should be kept.

## Why it matters

- Minutes are evidence of how decisions were made. A bank, auditor or court may ask for them.

Good minutes protect directors, so they should be written promptly. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Converting a partnership firm into a company or LLP in simple words
posts.excerpt: How an existing business can move into a company form.
posts.body:
A partnership firm can move into a company or an LLP, to get limited liability and a separate legal identity. The law has special provisions for this.

## To a company

- The Companies Act, 2013 allows a registered or unregistered firm to register as a company under Part I of Chapter XXI, subject to the conditions there.
- The partners become shareholders, and assets and liabilities pass to the company.

## To an LLP

- The LLP Act, 2008 has a schedule for conversion of a firm into an LLP.
- All partners generally need to agree and become partners of the LLP.

## Points to check

- Tax effects of the conversion under the Income-tax Act.
- Transfer of licences, registrations, bank accounts and contracts.
- Stamp duty and notifications to customers and authorities.

The tax treatment is important, so it should be examined before deciding. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Changing a company's registered office in simple words
posts.excerpt: What is needed to move the registered office.
posts.body:
Every company must have a registered office in India, to which communications can be sent. Section 12 of the Companies Act, 2013 deals with it.

## Within the same city

- A board resolution and a notice to the Registrar in the prescribed form are needed, within the time limit.

## Within the same state but another Registrar's jurisdiction

- A special resolution is usually needed, with a filing to the Registrar.

## To another state

- It involves an alteration of the memorandum, a special resolution and approval of the Central Government.
- Notice to creditors and others may be needed.

## Other updates

- Change the address on PAN, GST, bank, IEC and other registrations after the move.

The steps and forms differ by type of move, so the right one should be used. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Winding up a company in simple words
posts.excerpt: The main ways a company ends.
posts.body:
A company does not end just because it stops working. It has to be closed through a legal process.

## Strike-off

- For a company with no business and no debts. The Registrar removes its name from the register.

## Voluntary liquidation

- Under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, a solvent company can be wound up by its members through a liquidator.

## Insolvency

- If the company cannot pay its debts, creditors or the company can use the insolvency process before the National Company Law Tribunal.

## Points to remember

- Dues to employees, tax authorities and creditors have to be dealt with.
- Records must be kept for the period the law requires.

The right route depends on whether the company is solvent and on its debts. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Auditors of a company in simple words
posts.excerpt: Who appoints the auditor and for how long.
posts.body:
Most companies must appoint an auditor to examine their accounts. The rules are in Chapter X of the Companies Act, 2013.

## First auditor

- The board appoints the first auditor within the time allowed after incorporation. The auditor holds office until the first annual general meeting.

## Later appointments

- Shareholders appoint the auditor at the annual general meeting, generally for a term of five years.
- The auditor must give a written consent and certificate of eligibility.

## Points to remember

- Certain companies must rotate auditors after fixed terms.
- An auditor is filed with the Registrar in the prescribed form.

The auditor's independence is a legal requirement and should be respected. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Choosing a company name in simple words
posts.excerpt: What the Registrar looks at when approving a name.
posts.body:
The name of a company is approved by the Registrar of Companies under section 4 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014.

## Common rules

- The name must not be identical to or too like an existing company or LLP name.
- It must not be misleading or suggest a government connection or a prohibited use.
- It must end with 'Limited' or 'Private Limited', or the form allowed for its type.

## Trademark check

- A name that is too similar to a registered trademark may be objected to by the owner.
- A company name does not itself give trademark rights.

## Practical steps

- Search company and trademark records before choosing.
- Prepare a few alternatives.

Name approval is only the first step, so brand protection should also be considered. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Trademark classes in simple words
posts.excerpt: How goods and services are grouped for registration.
posts.body:
Trademarks are registered in classes. Under the Nice Classification there are 45 classes, 34 for goods and 11 for services.

## Why classes matter

- A registration protects the mark for the goods or services in the class applied for, and similar items.
- If your business spans more than one area, you may need to file in more than one class.

## Choosing the right class

- Describe the goods or services as precisely as you can.
- A class heading can be broad, and an application can be refused if the description is wrong or unclear.

## Costs

- The fee is charged per class, so the number of classes affects the cost.

A search of the classes before filing helps avoid mistakes. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Passing off in simple words
posts.excerpt: Protection for a brand even without registration.
posts.body:
Passing off is a common law remedy, which means it comes from court decisions. It protects a business against someone who presents goods or services as if they were those of another.

## What must be shown

- Goodwill or reputation in the name or get-up.
- A misrepresentation by the other side, likely to confuse customers.
- Damage or likely damage to the business.

## Relation to registration

- A registered trademark is easier to enforce, but passing off can be used for unregistered marks too, and also against a registered mark in some cases.
- The Trade Marks Act, 1999 recognises the common law rights in section 27(2).

## Evidence

- Sales figures, advertising, invoices and customer examples showing the use and reputation.

Records of use over time are the most useful evidence. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Copyright in software in simple words
posts.excerpt: How the law protects computer programs.
posts.body:
Under the Copyright Act, 1957, a computer program is treated as a literary work, and the code is protected from copying.

## What is protected

- The source code and object code as written.
- Not the idea, algorithm or method behind it, though a patent may be possible in some cases.

## Ownership

- The author is generally the first owner, but if it is created under a contract of service, the employer is generally the owner.
- For work done by an outside developer, ownership depends on the contract, so a written assignment is advisable.

## Uses

- Licences can give users the right to use the software on set terms.
- Open source licences have their own conditions.

A clear development agreement avoids disputes about who owns the code. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Who owns the IP: employees and contractors in simple words
posts.excerpt: How to avoid disputes over creations made for a business.
posts.body:
A common dispute arises when a business pays someone to create a logo, website, design or software, and later the two disagree on who owns it.

## Employees

- For works made in the course of employment under a contract of service, the employer is the first owner of copyright unless there is an agreement otherwise.
- Inventions are dealt with by the employment terms and by patent law.

## Contractors and freelancers

- Ownership may remain with the creator unless it is assigned in writing.
- The assignment should state what is transferred, for how long and where.

## What to put in an agreement

- Clear assignment or licence terms, confidentiality, and a promise that the work is original.

Papers signed at the start are easier than a dispute later. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Domain names and trademarks in simple words
posts.excerpt: How a website name relates to brand rights.
posts.body:
A domain name is a web address. It is registered with a registrar, and on a first-come basis, and does not by itself give trademark rights.

## The overlap

- A domain that copies someone else's trademark can lead to a dispute.
- Courts in India have treated domain names as capable of protection in passing off cases.

## Dispute resolution

- Disputes over .in domains can be taken to the .IN Domain Name Dispute Resolution Policy.
- For many other domains, the UDRP policy applies.

## Practical advice

- Search for existing trademarks before buying a domain.
- Register the brand as a trademark, if it will be used for business.

A domain and a trademark should be planned together. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 in simple words
posts.excerpt: How a consumer can raise a complaint.
posts.body:
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 protects buyers of goods and users of services from defective goods, deficient services and unfair trade practices.

## Who is a consumer

- A person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, generally not for resale or commercial purposes.

## Where to complain

- The District, State or National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, depending on the value of the claim as the law fixes.
- A complaint can be filed online through the e-Daakhil portal.

## Time limit

- A complaint should generally be filed within two years from when the cause of action arose.

## Other features

- The Act deals with product liability, misleading advertisement and e-commerce.

The pecuniary limits of each Commission are set by rules and have been revised. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Cheque dishonour under Section 138 in simple words
posts.excerpt: The steps after a cheque is returned unpaid.
posts.body:
When a cheque given for a debt or liability is returned by the bank for insufficient funds or similar reasons, section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 may apply.

## The timeline

- The cheque must be presented to the bank within its validity.
- After the bank's return memo, the holder must send a written demand notice within thirty days.
- The drawer has fifteen days after receiving it to pay.
- If no payment is made, a complaint can be filed in court within one month after those fifteen days end.

## What the court may do

- The offence is punishable with imprisonment or fine as the section provides.
- Courts encourage settlement, and compounding is possible.

## Evidence

- The cheque, return memo, notice, proof of delivery and proof of the debt.

The time limits are strict, so each step should be dated and recorded. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Limitation in simple words: how long you have to go to court
posts.excerpt: Why late claims can fail.
posts.body:
The Limitation Act, 1963 sets time limits within which a person must file a suit or appeal. After the period ends, the remedy can be lost even if the claim was good.

## Examples of general periods

- Many suits for recovery of money have a period of three years.
- Suits for possession of immovable property have longer periods, and appeals have shorter ones.

## When time starts

- Generally from the date the right to sue arises, and the Act sets the starting point for each case.

## Extensions

- Some provisions allow exclusion of time, such as time taken in a wrong court in good faith, and acknowledgement of a debt in writing can renew the period.
- Sufficient cause can excuse delay in appeals.

A matter should be examined early because the time starts to run from the cause of action. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: How a civil suit proceeds in simple words
posts.excerpt: The main stages from plaint to decree.
posts.body:
A civil suit follows the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The stages are in general the same for most suits.

## Stages

- Plaint: the claimant files a written statement of the claim.
- Summons: the defendant is called to appear and file a written statement.
- Issues: the court decides the points in dispute.
- Evidence: each side leads witnesses and documents.
- Arguments and judgment, followed by a decree.

## Along the way

- Interim orders such as injunctions can be sought in urgent cases.
- The court may refer the matter to mediation.

## After the decree

- An appeal or execution of the decree can follow.

Commercial suits above a stated value follow the Commercial Courts Act, which has its own timetable. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Arbitration in simple words
posts.excerpt: A private way of settling business disputes.
posts.body:
Arbitration is a method where the parties agree to have their dispute decided by an arbitrator and not by a court. It is governed by the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.

## How it starts

- The contract has an arbitration clause, or the parties later agree to arbitrate.
- One party gives notice invoking the clause, and the arbitrator is appointed as the clause provides.

## The award

- The arbitrator gives a written award, which is binding.
- A court can set it aside only on limited grounds.

## Points to include in a clause

- Number of arbitrators, the seat and place of arbitration, language, and the governing law.

A clearly drafted clause prevents a fight about the process itself. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: Power of attorney in simple words
posts.excerpt: Letting another person act for you.
posts.body:
A power of attorney is a document by which one person, the principal, authorises another, the agent, to act on his behalf. It is governed by the Powers of Attorney Act, 1882 and the Indian Contract Act, 1872.

## Types

- General: wide powers over many matters.
- Special: powers for a specific act, such as selling a particular property.

## Formalities

- It must be on proper stamp paper, as the state stamp law requires.
- For dealing with immovable property, registration is usually needed.
- A power of attorney signed outside India needs to be attested as the law requires.

## Points to remember

- The agent must act within the powers given.
- It can be cancelled by the principal in writing, and it ends on the principal's death.

The powers should be written in specific terms, never wider than needed. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.

posts.title: How to read a customs notification in simple words
posts.excerpt: A short guide to the parts of a notification and what they mean.
posts.body:
Customs duty rates and exemptions are set by notifications issued by the Ministry of Finance (CBIC). Reading them correctly saves money and trouble.

## Parts of a notification

- The number and year, and the date it comes into force.
- The power under which it is issued, such as section 25 of the Customs Act, 1962.
- The table of goods, with tariff heading, description, rate and conditions.

## Conditions

- A condition number in the table refers to a list of conditions at the end, for example about end use, certificates or a time limit.
- The benefit is lost if the condition is not met.

## Amendments

- A later notification can amend an earlier one, so the latest consolidated text should be used.
- Check the date of the import against the date of effect.

When the text is unclear, the department's circulars and past decisions can help. Rules, fees and time limits change, so the current law and official sources should always be checked.

This post is general information, not legal advice.
